extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy (readers of Kant / critical philosophy)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for assessing philosophical proofs and arguments about God, freedom, immortality, teleology, and the limits of theoretical vs practical Reason, as discussed in a Kantian critical philosophy context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief must be grounded upon facts
rubrics_metrics.description: All belief must in the first place be grounded upon facts, if it is not to be completely groundless; belief derived from facts can be grounded either as knowledge (theoretical cognition) or merely as faith (practical).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between theoretical proofs (knowledge founded on natural concepts and sense-experience) and practical proofs (faith grounded in the concept of freedom). Use this distinction to judge whether a purported proof provides theoretical cognition or only a practical warrant for belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faith as a moral, practical trust
rubrics_metrics.description: Faith is trust in the attainment of a design, the promotion of which is a duty; it is a free belief grounded in Reason only with respect to its practical employment, not supported by dogmatical theoretical proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat faith that refers to objects beyond possible knowledge as a moral, practical attitude rather than theoretical cognition; evaluate whether its grounding is adequate for practical ends (religion, moral purpose) rather than for speculative knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credulity versus faith (historical matters)
rubrics_metrics.description: When belief refers to particular objects which are not objects of possible knowledge or opinion—especially in historical matters—it ought to be called credulity and not faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid conflating mere credulity with morally justified faith; check whether the object of belief is amenable to possible knowledge/opinion before labeling it 'faith.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Dogmatical unbelief incompatible with moral maxim
rubrics_metrics.description: A dogmatical unbelief (denying validity to rational Ideas for want of theoretical ground) cannot subsist together with a moral maxim dominant in the mental attitude, whereas a doubtful faith can.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess consistency between an agent's professed moral commitments and their epistemic stance: if they demand obedience to a moral maxim, dogmatic denial of rational ideas that ground that maxim is incoherent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral concept of freedom as ground for cognizing supersensible
rubrics_metrics.description: The concept of freedom (as fundamental concept of all unconditioned practical laws) is the only concept of the supersensible which, by means of causality thought in it, proves its objective reality in nature through effects it can produce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating claims about God or the soul, consider whether appeal to freedom and moral causality supplies the only practical (not theoretical) ground for postulating supersensible realities; check for the practical effects claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theology and pneumatology cannot be established by empirical predicates
rubrics_metrics.description: Theology and Pneumatology, regarded as problems of speculative Reason, can be established by no empirical data and predicates, because the concept of them is transcendent for our whole cognitive faculty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject arguments that attempt to derive determinate concepts of God or the soul from empirical predicates alone; mark such efforts as inadequate for speculative/theoretical cognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ontological and metaphysico-cosmological proofs are insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments from purely ontological predicates or from the absolute necessity of some being are sophistical and cannot provide a determinate concept of an original Being available for cognition; such proofs cannot pass from schools into the world or influence common Understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat ontological-style demonstrations with suspicion: evaluate whether predicates used are only metaphysical and whether the argument illegitimately moves from concept to existence without empirical grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical (physico-teleological) proof limited to suggesting an intelligent cause
rubrics_metrics.description: The proof derived from the purposes of nature (physical teleology) can guide Reason to think an intelligent Cause of the world but cannot furnish a determinate concept of the original Being sufficient for Theology (it does not prove omniscience, omnipotence, uniqueness, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing design/teleological arguments, credit their power to incline ordinary Understanding toward an intelligent cause but not to establish a fully determinate theological concept; beware of inferring maximal perfections from empirical purposiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral teleology supplies determinate theological concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral Teleology, resting a priori on principles inseparable from Reason, leads to a determinate concept of the supreme Cause (an Author of the world) adequate for Theology, supplying properties such as Omniscience, Omnipotence, Omnipresence as necessary to the moral final purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give moral arguments primacy when the aim is a concept of God adequate for religion: evaluate whether the argument links moral final ends and obligation to the attributes ascribed to a supreme Cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion requires theology insofar as it supports practical moral use
rubrics_metrics.description: Theology is not needed for extension or correction of cognition of nature but is subjectively required for Religion—the practical or moral use of Reason—because the concept of God arising from moral Ideas supports our moral destination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge theological claims by their sufficiency to support practical moral ends (recognition of duties as divine commands), not by their speculative extension of natural knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theological ethics (laws not given by Reason) are not moral
rubrics_metrics.description: A Theological Ethic (of pure Reason) is impossible; laws which Reason itself does not give and whose observance it does not bring about as a pure practical faculty cannot be moral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject as genuinely moral any ethical system whose laws are externally imposed (theological ordinances) rather than arising from practical Reason itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories (e.g., causality) only apply to objects of possible experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Categories (such as causality) have no significance for theoretical cognition when applied to supersensible objects; applying the category of causality to a supersensible first mover leaves the concept empty and does not cognise what God is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating claims that use conceptual categories to describe God or other supersensible entities, check whether those categories presuppose conditions of possible experience; if so, regard the attribution as non-cognitive in the theoretical sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy allows thinking God-as-intelligence for practical but not theoretical cognition
rubrics_metrics.description: By analogy to an Understanding we can think a supersensible being as intelligence in a practical employment of Reason (to provide a concept for moral purposes), but this does not imply theoretical cognition of God's nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow analogical reasoning to justify practical postulates (e.g., for religion and moral purpose) but mark it as insufficient for claiming theoretical knowledge of divine attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical data cannot establish uniqueness of the original Being without arbitrary addition
rubrics_metrics.description: From empirical purposiveness one cannot infer a unique intelligent original Being; to arrive at uniqueness one must arbitrarily add the assumption that all perfections are united in a unique Cause merely for the better employment of Reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag arguments that move from empirical evidence to claims of a uniquely perfect Deity as relying on extra-empirical assumptions; require explicit recognition of any such arbitrary interpolations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical teleology may be propaedeutic but cannot replace moral proof
rubrics_metrics.description: A physico-teleological Theology can serve as a propaedeutic to Theology proper by giving occasion for the idea of a final purpose, but it cannot develop or satisfactorily ground Theology; moral proof remains necessary for theological adequacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In pedagogy or argumentative sequencing, treat design/teleological arguments as preparatory aids that make the mind receptive to moral proofs, not as substitutes for moral/theological justification.
